fatal_errors: The proposed forging-and-annealing intervention is unrelated to the target comparison of Ta-to-Ti substitution, hybrid MD/MC atom swaps, mechanical alloying, and spark-plasma sintering.
The assumed coherent precipitate network is not established for the unspecified tungsten-based refractory HEA; the cited precipitate evidence concerns a different FCC/L12 high-entropy superalloy.
The thermal-transport mechanism overemphasizes phonon scattering at grain boundaries even though electronic transport and chemical-disorder scattering are central in metallic refractory HEAs.
No cited evidence directly supports improved thermal conductivity from the proposed forging and short annealing treatment.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the general reactor-interlayer objective and proposes a controlled treated-versus-untreated test, but it does not reconstruct the target material system, intervention, phase evolution, or measured outcome. The target found predominantly bcc-derived CrFeTaVW and CrFeTiVW structures, alloy-specific segregation and Laves-phase formation, similar low diffusivity for Ta- and Ti-containing compositions, and only a modest temperature-driven diffusivity increase. In contrast, the generated hypothesis assumes an unspecified W–Mo–Nb–Ta alloy, coherent strengthening precipitates, and conductivity enhancement through grain alignment and coarsening. Its service-temperature range only partly overlaps the target measurement range, and loading conditions are not quantified. The experiment could reveal a conductivity-strength trade-off, but forging and annealing parameters, alloy composition, statistical design, heat-flux conditions, and quantitative acceptance thresholds are missing. The cited studies support the need for interlayers and the general high-temperature strength of some HEAs, not the proposed processing–microstructure–conductivity chain.
